summaries.headline: IBM, Microsoft Launch Enterprise AI Agent Platform
summaries.summary: IBM and Microsoft have unveiled Imagine Enterprise, a platform combining more than 6,000 pre-built AI agents from IBM Consulting with Microsoft's AI, data, cloud and security tools, initially aimed at financial services, insurance and retail organizations. The platform includes enterprise identity, security and governance controls, with forward-deployed engineers from both companies supporting qualifying customer implementations; financial firm SEI is cited as an early exploratory partner, though no completed deployment or measured results are reported. The announcement signals how major tech vendors are packaging agentic AI for regulated industries with heavy compliance needs, a model district technology leaders may see echoed as K-12-focused vendors build similar agent-based offerings.

summaries.headline: OpenAI Expands External Security Testing With Hacktron
summaries.summary: OpenAI has partnered with Hacktron to jointly select priority security tests focused on how its systems connect with third-party services, expanding on work that began through OpenAI's bug bounty program. Hacktron will gain broader access to OpenAI's frontier models through Daybreak Red, building on prior research where its investigators chained two bugs to reach employee ChatGPT and Codex accounts in under 72 hours. For districts relying on AI tools that integrate with other platforms, the move signals that even leading AI developers see interconnected systems — not standalone models — as the primary security risk to watch.

summaries.headline: Illinois Funding Formula Shields Districts From Tax Credit Fallout
summaries.summary: Teachers unions oppose Illinois joining the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit, warning that student departures to private schools would drain public school funding, but the state's Evidence-Based Funding formula includes a hold-harmless provision guaranteeing districts receive at least as much state money as the prior year regardless of enrollment shifts. Cicero Public School District 99 illustrates the mechanism in action: despite losing over 1,300 students between 2021 and 2025, the district has continued to receive $120 million annually in EBF funds, with per-pupil spending actually climbing by nearly $6,500. Enrollment still factors into how new EBF dollars get distributed through each district's Adequacy Target, but a built-in lag using prior-year or three-year average enrollment means shrinking districts keep drawing on higher enrollment figures for a time — leaving the central claim that public schools would lose funding unsupported by the formula's actual design.

summaries.headline: New Tools Target Teen Health Misinformation
summaries.summary: The News Literacy Project has released new classroom resources aimed at helping students evaluate health and science claims circulating on social media, from nutrition fads to pseudoscience trends. The hub includes a five-week "Brain Gains" planner with interactive lessons and printable posters covering source credibility, data analysis, and algorithm literacy, alongside a mnemonic-based poster for assessing verification, accuracy, independence, transparency, fairness and accountability in any source. As teens increasingly encounter health claims through social feeds rather than traditional outlets, these free, ready-to-use materials give teachers a concrete entry point for embedding media literacy into existing instruction.

summaries.headline: Newark Coalition Targets Third-Grade Reading Proficiency
summaries.summary: My Brother's Keeper Newark has launched an "Early Literacy Anchor Table," convening government, education, and community leaders to build a data-driven ecosystem aimed at getting third graders reading at grade level. The initiative, led with Newark Opportunity Youth Network and backed by Rutgers University—Newark's Cornwall Center for data analysis, explicitly borrows its model from the city's public safety strategy, which Mayor Ras Baraka credits with a 55 percent decrease in homicides between 2013 and 2022. The approach signals a bet that cross-sector, data-sharing collaboratives built for crime reduction can be repurposed to close literacy gaps, with findings expected to shape evidence-based strategies in Newark schools serving third graders.

summaries.headline: Newark Test Scores Diverge, But Comparisons Get Complicated
summaries.summary: Newark's 2025-26 state test results show English proficiency dropping to 35.7% from 41.7% while math proficiency climbed to 30.1% from 27%, but New Jersey's shift to adaptive testing with new proficiency standards makes year-over-year comparisons unreliable, state officials caution. Charter schools significantly outpaced district schools across both subjects — 46% to 29% in English and 41.4% to 22.5% in math — while district middle schoolers struggled most, with just 14% of eighth graders meeting grade-level math expectations. District officials point to growth data showing roughly two-thirds of students made typical or high progress in math as a more meaningful measure than proficiency alone, but State Board of Education members are already pushing for closer scrutiny of the tutoring and literacy investments meant to drive pandemic recovery.

summaries.headline: CTU-Backed Candidates Secure Chicago School Board Wins
summaries.summary: Chicago voters have settled three of four contested school board races more than a week after Election Day, with CTU-backed candidates Jason Dónes, Michilla Blaise, and Emma Lozano all winning their districts. Dónes unseated incumbent Carlos Rivas Jr. with 52% of the vote despite being outspent by pro-school choice groups and an anti-CTU PAC funded by billionaire Michael Sacks, while Lozano held off a challenger backed by nearly every major education group besides the union, 54% to 46%. The results confirm that candidates aligned with school choice groups will still hold a narrow majority on the city's first fully elected board, even as CTU's ground game proved decisive in several close contests — a split outcome that leaves the board's governing dynamics far from settled as the Nov. 24 certification approaches.

summaries.headline: California Bars Ed-Tech Vendors From Training AI on Student Data
summaries.summary: California Governor Newsom signed AB 1159, amending KOPIPA and ELPIPA and creating a new Higher Education Student Information Protection Act, with K-12 provisions taking effect January 1, 2027, and higher-ed provisions beginning July 1, 2027. The law prohibits operators and their subcontractors from using student data to train generative AI systems, bans collection or disclosure of data on reproductive health, immigration status, sexual orientation, or gender identity, requires written data retention policies, and creates a private right of action letting students or parents sue for actual damages or $500 per violation after a 60-day cure period. For district leaders, the expanded definition of "operator" now pulls vendors and subcontractors into scope, meaning contract reviews, AI-use disclosures, and indemnity provisions will need updating well before the 2027 deadlines.

summaries.headline: Chegg Settlements Expose Student Data, Billing Risks
summaries.summary: Chegg's legal history offers a cautionary tale for any district evaluating ed-tech vendors, with the company settling FTC charges for $7.5 million over "dark pattern" billing practices that made it hard for students to cancel subscriptions. A separate 2018 breach exposed roughly 40 million user accounts after Chegg stored passwords with outdated MD5 hashing, prompting an FTC consent order mandating multi-factor authentication, staff security training, and strict data-minimization rules. For leaders vetting homework-help and study platforms, the case underscores why contract review should include scrutiny of auto-renewal terms, encryption standards, and data retention policies before students' personal and financial information is on the line.

summaries.headline: Arizona Districts Fight Stubborn Post-Pandemic Absenteeism
summaries.summary: Nearly 25% of Arizona students in grades 1-8 were chronically absent in 2025, according to the Helios Education Foundation, still nearly double the 13% rate recorded in 2019, and the state's own research ties chronic absence directly to lower math and ELA performance. Buckeye Elementary School District has pushed its rate down to 19.35%, below the state average, using a homegrown early-warning tool called Attend33 that measures absences against actual school session days and feeds staff sortable, actionable data rather than static spreadsheets, paired with tiered action plans built at every school. Nonprofits like Valley of the Sun United Way are betting that relationship-based outreach, rather than punitive tracking, combined with addressing root causes like housing instability and healthcare access, is what will determine whether these gains hold as rates have already rebounded once since the pandemic.

summaries.headline: South Bend School Cuts Chronic Absenteeism by 26 Points
summaries.summary: Marshall Traditional School in South Bend, Indiana, saw its chronic absenteeism rate drop to 9.7% in 2025-26 from 36.4% the prior year, according to Indiana Department of Education data. Principal Amanda Choinacky credits the turnaround to an all-hands-on-deck approach centered on relationship-building, arguing that strong tier-one instruction means little if students aren't in the building to receive it. The gains extended beyond one school: South Bend Community School Corporation posted a 6-percentage-point drop in chronic absenteeism district-wide, suggesting that a relational, belonging-focused strategy can move attendance numbers at scale, not just in isolated classrooms.

summaries.headline: New Consortium to Test if AI Learning Sticks
summaries.summary: UCLA researcher Tina Austin has launched an international consortium, drawing interest from more than 40 institutions, to examine whether AI-supported learning builds skills students actually retain once the technology is removed. Austin argues existing research on both sides of the AI debate has methodological gaps: studies claiming harm often skip assessing students' baseline capabilities or preparation, while studies claiming benefits frequently measure performance only while AI support is still active, rarely testing what persists weeks or months later. The consortium will build on her Metacognitive Awareness Scale and UnBlooms framework to track how students' reasoning changes across subjects, offering leaders a more rigorous basis for deciding which AI practices and assessments actually translate into independent student understanding.

summaries.headline: Stanford Launches Five-Year AI Brain-Modeling Project
summaries.summary: Stanford University has launched a five-year initiative, the Stanford Digital Brain Project, bringing together faculty from its Humanities and Sciences, Medicine and Engineering schools to build AI foundation models that predict how the human brain responds across perception, memory, language, emotion and reasoning. Researchers will combine 7-tesla MRI scans with wearable OPM-MEG recordings and Stanford's Marlowe GPU computing cluster, starting with models of individual brain systems before expanding toward whole-brain models, with potential applications in identifying early biomarkers for disorders like depression and Parkinson's disease. Stanford plans to release the resulting datasets and models freely to researchers worldwide, extending existing open platforms like OpenNeuro — a long-term bet that foundation-model approaches to neuroscience could eventually inform how brain-based conditions affecting learning and behavior are understood and treated.

summaries.headline: Accenture Taps AWS Veteran to Lead OpenAI Push
summaries.summary: Accenture has hired former AWS executive Richard Halkett as Managing Director and OpenAI Enterprise Reinvention Group Lead for North America, tasking him with helping organizations translate AI capabilities into operational change. The move builds on Accenture's position as one of four firms—alongside Capgemini, Boston Consulting Group, and McKinsey—named to OpenAI's Frontier Alliances in February 2026, with Accenture reporting 52,000 professionals already using ChatGPT Enterprise and pursuing OpenAI certifications. For district leaders watching how major consultancies structure AI deployment and workforce training at scale, this signals where corporate playbooks on AI adoption and employee upskilling are heading.

summaries.headline: West Virginia Seeks $410 Million Funding Fix
summaries.summary: The West Virginia Department of Education presented lawmakers a nine-point proposal to overhaul the state's decades-old school funding formula, estimating an additional $410 million is needed to meet current student needs. Special education tops the list at $189 million, driven by a jump in special ed enrollment from just over 14 percent to over 21 percent of students, with $63.9 million more sought for low-income weighted funding and additional dollars for stabilizing enrollment-based allocations amid population loss — 3,000 children left the state during the 2025-2026 school year. With a lawsuit threat and the governor predicting the issue will "dominate" the 2027 legislative session, the proposal sets up a high-stakes funding debate over whether incremental fixes can keep pace with rising student needs and shrinking enrollment.

summaries.headline: West Virginia Weighs $410 Million School Funding Overhaul
summaries.summary: West Virginia education officials briefed lawmakers on draft legislation to replace the state's enrollment-based school aid formula with a weighted model tied to student needs, as falling enrollment collides with rising costs for special education and rural students. The proposal carries an estimated $410 million annual price tag on top of the current $1.4 billion, driven partly by special education enrollment projected to jump from 15.3% to 21.4% of students by 2027, and would overhaul personnel allowances, low-enrollment county thresholds, and transportation and facilities funding. With enrollment down 3.5% this year alone and courts potentially forcing changes regardless, the Legislature now faces a choice between funding a more precise formula or risking a judicial mandate that offers less control over the details.

summaries.headline: Young Workers Hit Hardest in AI-Exposed Jobs
summaries.summary: Stanford Digital Economy Lab's new Canaries Dashboard finds workers aged 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations, including software development and customer service, are seeing employment declines at a 4.4% annual rate in recent months, while older workers in the same fields show growth or stability. The data, built with ADP Research payroll records, shows the pattern weakens with age and correlates with "automation" use (full task delegation to AI) more than "augmentation" (human-AI collaboration), though the lab stops short of claiming AI caused the declines. Stanford Accelerator for Learning's Isabelle Hau is using the findings to push for new apprenticeship, mentorship and experiential learning models, arguing that schools must now deliberately teach relational intelligence, judgment and adaptability rather than assume students pick them up on the job.

summaries.headline: Memrise Founders' New Startup Raises Pre-Seed Funding
summaries.summary: Mindmax, founded by Memrise creators Ed Cooke and Daniel Zohar, has raised £2.5 million in pre-seed funding led by Concept Ventures for an AI tutor built around real-time, interruptible conversation rather than one-way video or classroom instruction. The app targets professional exam preparation and upskilling first, planning adaptive daily lessons that track a learner's mistakes and goals, with a companion coach delivering check-ins to re-engage users who fall off their study plan. The company claims its interactive approach outperforms traditional formats, but the announcement includes no exam pass rates, retention data, or other outcome measures to support that comparison.

summaries.headline: School Funding Formulas Haven't Caught Up to Enrollment Decline
summaries.summary: Public schools have lost 1.4 million students since 2020 and are projected to lose another 2.7 million by 2031-32, yet many state funding formulas still rely on prior-year or multi-year enrollment counts that pay districts for "ghost students" no longer in classrooms. Missouri's declining-enrollment provision cost the state an extra $197 million in 2022, and California's hold-harmless policy ran an estimated $4 billion in 2023, even though California funds its charter schools using current-year counts without issue. As school choice programs expand and dollars increasingly need to follow individual students, states clinging to outdated counting methods risk both budget strain and misaligned incentives for districts to adapt to shrinking rolls.

summaries.headline: Arizona's Literacy Push Gains Ground, Gap Persists
summaries.summary: Arizona is working to lift its third-grade reading pass rate from 40% to 72% by 2030 under the AZ Literacy Plan 2030, led by Read On Arizona, and officials say early indicators are moving in the right direction even as the state remains far from its target. The number of literacy coaches placed in schools has grown from about 24 to nearly 40, still well short of the initiative's goal of 125, while the share of educators holding a K-5 literacy endorsement has jumped from 12% to a projected 31%. With this year's assessment results not yet available, the state's progress will hinge on whether gains in coaching capacity and educator credentialing translate into actual reading outcomes for students.

House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter has reappointed Rep. Danny Garrett, R-Trussville, as chairman of the House Ways and Means Education Committee, which oversees the development of Alabama’s Education Trust Fund budget.

Garrett has chaired the committee since 2021, overseeing five record-setting education budgets that have included increases in teacher pay and funding for K-12 schools, community colleges and public universities.

“The last four years have been the most transformative period in state history for public education, and much of that success can be directly traced back to Chairman Garrett’s leadership,” Ledbetter said in a news release announcing the reappointment.

Garrett has helped develop budgets that included four teacher pay raises since 2022. He also supported legislation establishing paid parental leave for public education employees in 2025.

Garrett played a role in the passage of the CHOOSE Act, Alabama’s education savings account program, which lawmakers approved in 2024. The program began providing funding for private school tuition and other qualifying education expenses during the 2025-26 school year.

Garrett credited the state’s recent academic gains in part to the committee’s approach to education spending.

“For the first time in our state’s history, Alabama is leading the nation in learning gains while setting a strong example for others to follow, and that starts with conservative budgeting in our committee.

“At the end of the day, every decision we make is guided by the fact that this is not the state government’s money – it belongs to Alabama’s children, and I remain committed to ensuring it is spent in a manner that gives them the best possible opportunity to succeed,” Garrett said.

A decade ago, West Virginia schools had more than 44,000 special education students.

Today, that number exceeds 48,000, about 21% of all public school students. This comes even as student enrollment overall has plummeted by 17% in the same time period, according to the state Department of Education.

LAURA BILSON \| Gazette-Mail

That is the crux of the problem with how West Virginia funds its schools, according to Uriah Cummings, a school financial operations officer at the West Virginia Department of Education. There are fewer students overall, but the ones who remain need more help and more resources. Addressing that disparity is one of the main goals of a new funding proposal the Department detailed during a meeting of the Legislature's Joint Committee on Education on Monday.

“It’s not about just asking for more money, in terms of what needs exist across the state of West Virginia,” Cummings said during his presentation to the Committee. “It’s being able to look at the current model that we have and saying, 'Is this model sufficient in terms of what it takes to educate a child in today’s day and age?’”

The answer to that question comes with a price, though — about $410 million, according to the department.

### Fumbling with the funding

There is broad recognition that the state needs to change how it funds its 55 school districts. The current system is based heavily on headcount, so as the number of pupils drops, districts receive less money, leading to layoffs and school closures. It also does not account for whether students are low-income or have other special education or English language learning needs, despite those students needing more resources.

[The state is already facing at least one lawsuit over the system](https://www.wvgazettemail.com/news/legal_affairs/officials-ask-wvs-top-court-for-more-time-on-school-funding-lawsuit-cite-2027-session/article_7ac9ca61-4d0b-4aac-bf39-de0435980e29.html). During last month’s state Board of Education meeting, the board acknowledged that the current funding system is “inadequate” and does not allow them to fulfill their duty of managing the state’s public schools.

The current proposal would, among other things, weigh special needs students more heavily when calculating how much money districts get as a way to compensate for the additional costs it takes to educate them. According to the Board of Education, federal funding [only covers 12% to 17% of the costs](https://wvde.us/articles/wv-board-ed-takes-position-school-funding-formula-inadequate) of counties’ special education needs.

The Board is also pushing for changes in how enrollment is funded as a way to help shield districts from sudden headcount drops. The [current idea would allow districts to use either prior year’s numbers or a three-year average, whichever is higher](https://wvde.us/media/10074/uriah-cummings-boardmembersummarypsspmodernizationpdf).

Several lawmakers on Monday brought up the estimated $410 million cost.

“I think we still have a lot to unravel when it comes to this proposal. It’s gonna create questions when it comes to a price tag that high,” said Delegate Jimmy Willis, R-Brooke. He acknowledged, though, that the funding formula needs to be fixed and was glad to finally see options being presented.

Sen. Amy Grady, R-Mason, chair of the Senate Education Committee, said she wasn’t surprised by the price tag given the scope of the proposed changes, but she said it would take time for other members to digest the ideas and decide what to do. She didn’t rule out taking up parts of the proposal or doing it in a piecemeal way.

“I would love to say that we can do something. I’m really hopeful,” Grady said. “But I’m only one member out of 134.” She added that fixing the special education funding portion was a major priority for her personally.

Delegate Mike Pushkin, D-Kanawha, questioned how the new model would limit the raft of school closures that has ravaged districts across the state for years.

“I’m tired of seeing schools close. It makes the problem worse,” he said. “We talk about population loss, but nobody is gonna move to a state where they can’t get their kids to a school in the neighborhood they live in.”

Cummings responded that he hopes the change in how enrollment is funded by allowing schools to take the average of the past three years would help slow school closures. He added, though, that “there does come a time when it’s fiscal inefficiency” to run schools with low enrollment.

# Measure ES fails, leaving council with $12 million school funding choice

By [Matthew Hall](https://www.smdp.com/author/matthew-hall/)

![Measure ES fails, leaving council with $12 million school funding choice](https://storage.ghost.io/c/55/9f/559f9abc-8372-4a2e-8c2d-27386da4e363/content/images/size/w30/2026/11/Measure_ES_padded.png)

Santa Monica voters have rejected Measure ES, a citizen-initiated parcel tax that would have raised about $12 million a year for the Santa Monica-Malibu Unified School District, leaving the City Council to decide whether to end its annual payment to the district or find the money elsewhere.

The “no” votes had 52.5% of the ballot (20,014 votes) as of the most recent update compared to 47.5% “yes” (18,098) votes.

The results have yet to be certified but there are only a few hundred outstanding votes for the City of Santa Monica, far too few to overcome the current results. Certification is not expected until Nov. 27.

Measure ES would have imposed a special tax of $495 per taxable parcel, adjusted each year for inflation, with no expiration date. Qualifying seniors, affordable housing, nonprofits, religious organizations and schools would have been exempt.

All of the revenue would have gone to SMMUSD or a successor Santa Monica school district, with none going to a new Malibu district. The money could not have been used for administrator salaries, land purchases or new construction, and independent audits would have been required.

According to the City Attorney's impartial analysis, the measure was intended to replace city funding the district receives under the Master Facilities Use Agreement, which expires June 30, 2027. Because it qualified by petition, with 7,711 valid signatures, it needed only a simple majority to pass.

The initiative followed a January decision by city staff to pull a council-sponsored $540 parcel tax that would have required a two-thirds vote. A city poll of 499 voters in October 2025 showed weak support, with funding the school agreement ranking last of 10 uses tested, at 34%.

Supporters included the Santa Monica-Malibu Classroom Teachers Association, the Santa Monica Chamber of Commerce, the SMMUSD Council of PTAs, the SMMUSD board, Mayor Caroline Torosis and Councilmember Barry Snell. They argued the city's fiscal distress put the $12 million at risk.

Opponents, including Northeast Neighbors, the Wilshire Montana Neighborhood Coalition and the Pico Neighborhood Association, called ES "a Santa Monica City tax disguised as a school tax." They argued it would shift the cost from the city to residents permanently and free up $12 million in city money with "no restrictions."

In a statement, SMMUSD board President Alicia Mignano said the district "respects the voice of Santa Monica voters and the democratic process."

"The District remains committed to serving students, families, staff and the community," Mignano said. "We will continue to carefully assess our financial outlook and explore available options. This includes opportunities to collaborate with the City of Santa Monica as we move forward while keeping our community informed as we plan for the future."

She added that the district's priority "remains providing students with high-quality educational opportunities and maintaining strong schools and services for our community."

ES revenue would not have gone into the city's General Fund. But it would have let the council negotiate a successor agreement with the district without General Fund cost, and the city's budget projections already assume the roughly $12 million annual payment ends in 2027.

The City of Santa Monica did not respond to a request for comment by press time but staff have previously said any budget projections that lifted the city out of its current fiscal crisis were predicated on termination of the payment.

An October city staff report said that if voters rejected ES, the city planned to end the payment. In September, the council voted 6-0 to direct Chi to negotiate a successor agreement and to bring "the trade-offs that we will have to make if Measure ES does not pass" to a March 2027 budget study session. The next two-year budget takes effect July 1, 2027.

Keeping the payment would reopen a recurring gap of about $12 million. City year-end figures released in October show the city used $26.7 million in one-time reserves in fiscal year 2025-26, and the operating budget ran a $4.3 million deficit excluding $22.5 million in transfers to capital projects.

For the district, losing the payment would cut about 7% of its main operating revenue, according to supporters. SMMUSD already projected deficits of $9 million to $12 million a year through 2028-29, assuming the city kept paying. The district holds about $89 million in reserves.

The city will continue sending about $18 million a year to SMMUSD through a separate Measure YY/GS facilities agreement that runs through June 30, 2038.

(Photo courtesy University of Maine Cooperative Extension/Edwin Remsberg)](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/outdoor-funding-2-color.jpg)](https://lcnme.com/368642/announcements/umaine-extension-announces-outdoor-school-funding-opportunity/#photo)

Students collect river samples at the University of Maine 4-H Camp and Learning Center at Bryant Pond in Woodstock. The University of Maine Cooperative Extension opened the grant application period for Outdoor School providers on Friday, Nov. 6. Grants of up to $410 per student are available. (Photo courtesy University of Maine Cooperative Extension/Edwin Remsberg)

University of Maine Cooperative Extension has announced a new round of funding for the Outdoor School for All program, which provides immersive outdoor education experiences for students in grades four through eight.

The application portal for the 2026-2027 school year opened Friday, Nov. 6, with applications due Friday, Nov. 20.

Grants are available to eligible Maine nonprofit outdoor education organizations that provide these experiences to students attending publicly funded schools.

Established by the Maine Legislature in 2025 and administered by UMaine Extension, the program connects students with hands-on learning opportunities focused on science, technology, engineering, mathematics, environmental sustainability, and the state’s natural resource industries.

BELOIT — After 16 years of Republican or divided control, on Jan. 4, Democrats will hold the majority in the state Senate and Assembly and hold the Governor’s office.

This Democratic trifecta along with a majority on the Wisconsin Supreme Court is likely to mean significant changes to property taxes, reproductive rights, and the still controversial Act 10 that stripped most public workers of collective bargaining rights. In Beloit, though, perhaps the No. 1 issue may be what the new majority does when it comes to school funding and school choice.

Over the last 11 years, the School District of Beloit’s enrollment has declined from 7,022 in 2014-2015 to just 4,471, according to the numbers the district provided to the state at the end of September.

That decline in part is because of the national trend of families just having fewer children. The general fertility rate in the U.S. has declined every year since 2007. Another major factor, though, are the various programs allowing parents to choose the schools their children attend regardless of what district where they live.

This year, the School District of Beloit had 955 of its potential students choose to schools outside the Beloit school district just 96 who chose Beloit schools over their home district. The biggest beneficiary is Beloit Turner School District, which had 573 students opt in to their schools against 112 choosing to go elsewhere.

The Wisconsin Parental Choice Program was launched in 2013 and allowed families who met income qualifications to attend a participating private or religious school of their choice tuition free. Both Our Lady of the Assumption and Rock County Christian Schools in Beloit are in the voucher program.

Wisconsin first passed legislation allowing public charter schools in 1993 and in 2015 the legislature passed Act 55, which significantly expanded independent charter school authorization across the state. The Lincoln Academy, an independent, tuition-free public charter school, opened on Henry Avenue in Beloit in the fall of 2021 and this year it has 737 students.

In February, The Lincoln Academy’s board of directors approved a 145,000-square-foot expansion that will double the school’s size. It will be the biggest building project in the City of Beloit this decade except for the Ho-Chunk casino, hotel, convention center project.

In April, Rock County Christian purchased the 114,000-square-foot former McNeel Intermediate School from Beloit School District for $710,000 and began work on the building so RCCS could combine its two campuses in Beloit and Janesville.

The School District of Beloit board, meanwhile, held a series of meetings over the summer about future enrollment projections and last month publicly discussed plans that would close two to five of its buildings because of expected student declines. Now, the shifting political atmosphere adds a new variable to those talks.

“Some of the changes that are likely coming, like putting more state money in towards funding special education, aren’t that controversial,” said Laura Grube, an economics and business professor at Beloit College who helps coordinate the Beloit Public Library’s Civics Academy. “Some of the other proposals would cause major disruption and voters showed in this last election that they are paying attention.”

A week before the midterm election, State Sen. Mark Spreitzer at a voter forum held at Rock County Christian said he would vote to eliminate the voucher system if the question were put before him. Spreitzer will now be the Senate President.

Spreitzer recently told the Daily News he would like to put limits on the voucher system as it gradually winds down statewide. An example of limits he would like to see is reinstating the income qualifications for families granted vouchers.

Several state legislators, including Sen. Kelda Roys and Rep. Francesca Hong, who narrowly lost the Democratic nomination for Governor, pledged to sunset or phase out the voucher system. New Governor-elect David Crowly, though, doesn’t support ending the voucher program, saying immediate elimination would be impractical, and instead would maintain the system at its current size.

How that plays out will be critical for RCCS. This year, RCCS reported an enrollment of 227 students between its two campuses, about 85% of them are there on vouchers.

RCCS Board President Jon Urish said school administrators believe consolidating operations at McNeel will insulate RCCS even if the voucher system is scrapped or scaled back.

“We’re well aware of the broad range of public opinions about the school choice program,” Urish said in an email. “One of RCCS’s existing and ongoing goals is to become less reliant on the choice program, and we’re confident the move to our new campus is a big step in that direction. By consolidating two campuses into one, we gain some great operational efficiencies and give ourselves room to grow more methodically.”

The rules for charter schools also will be up for debate. An idea batted around that would affect TLA, requiring independent charter schools such as TLA to be linked to a public school district or community college, has lost steam. Instead, representatives such as Angelina Cruz of Racine and Joe Sheehan of Sheboygan have consistently opposed expanding funding for charter schools and want to require them to have the same transparency, reporting and academic standards as traditional public schools.

Lisa Furseth, executive director of the Hendricks Family Foundation and Chair of the Lincoln Academy Board of Directors, said she did not want to speculate on policies proposals until they are fully formulated and introduced.

“If legislation is introduced that could affect The Lincoln Academy, we will evaluate the specific proposal and its potential impact on scholars, families and educational opportunities,” Furseth said in an email. “At this point, our focus remains on supporting The Lincoln Academy and the opportunities it provides to young people in Beloit.”

Beloit School Board President Tia Johnson said the leadership change in Madison is something Beloit schools will have to consider.

“I am going to have a discussion with (Beloit Interim Superintendent Leah Gordon) about perhaps slowing down some of our talks while this all gets worked out,” Johnson said. “You don’t want to all of a sudden need more space because you sold all of your buildings.”

Over the 16 years since Democrats last had full control in Wisconsin, the School District of Beloit built one new school, Fran Fruzen Intermediate, and closed five, Royce, Wright and Morgan, Cunningham and McNeel. The district eventually sold Royce, Morgan and McNeel and has approved a sale of Wright. The district currently is holding onto Cunningham as the board considers future configurations.

Johnson said most of what the board discussed this summer needs addressing immediately.

“Unless we pass a referendum in April, we’re going to need make more budget cuts next fall and changes to state funding and rules aren’t going to happen over night,” Johnson said.

Interestingly, there seems to be no groundswell to change the open enrollment system, which particularly benefits Turner. Turner Superintendent Dennis McCarthy said he hopes legislators tackle three things:

\\* Increasing special education funding.

“With (state) reimbursement rates sitting in the 30-30% range in recent years, districts are forced to divert significant funding from their general fund to cover these needed services.”

\\* Changing the per pupil revenue limit disparities, which were aligned to 1993 funding levels and then decoupled from having to match the rate of inflation in 2009.

“(Beloit Turner School District) sits in the bottom 5% in per pupil revenue limit formula funding and that does not seem reasonable,” McCarthy said. “Our taxpayers need to know that our resident students simply are not funded fairly based on where they live in accordance with the state funding formula and revenue limits.”

\\* Put more money into the equalization aid formula.

“The real issue is the effort by legislators in refusing to put any new money into the equalization aid formula over the last two years,” McCarthy said. “Had that been done, local taxpayers throughout the state by and large would be paying less for local school support than they are now. The state needs to step up and do their part instead of making our public school districts a pawn to partisan politics.”

There seems to be no question that more money will be invested into public schools in the coming years. Crowley campaigned on moving the state toward a 90% reimbursement rate for special education costs, shifting a greater share of public school funding from local property taxes to the state, and forming a “blue ribbon commission” to completely overhaul the state’s school funding formula.

Grube said it is more likely that if there are sweeping changes it will be to school funding and just tweaks to the rules around the voucher system and charter schools.

“Polls consistently show that there is broad support for the school choice programs in Wisconsin,” Grube said. “For the families that use vouchers, or open enrollment or have their kids at a charter school, education is likely their No. 1 issue. If that gets taken away from them, the lesson from this election is that voters will change parties if an issue is important enough.”

# 'Hope and joyful expectation' as £23.3m Eyemouth Primary School funding agreed

By Paul Kelly

[Share to Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=2093404634019983&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.northumberlandgazette.co.uk%2Fnews%2Fpolitics%2Fcouncil%2Fhope-and-joyful-expectation-as-ps233m-eyemouth-primary-school-funding-agreed-9349605)[Share to X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=%E2%80%98Hope%20and%20joyful%20expectation%E2%80%99%C2%A0as%20%C2%A323.3m%20school%20funding%20is%20agreed&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.northumberlandgazette.co.uk%2Fnews%2Fpolitics%2Fcouncil%2Fhope-and-joyful-expectation-as-ps233m-eyemouth-primary-school-funding-agreed-9349605)[Share to WhatsApp](https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=%E2%80%98Hope%20and%20joyful%20expectation%E2%80%99%C2%A0as%20%C2%A323.3m%20school%20funding%20is%20agreed%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.northumberlandgazette.co.uk%2Fnews%2Fpolitics%2Fcouncil%2Fhope-and-joyful-expectation-as-ps233m-eyemouth-primary-school-funding-agreed-9349605&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.northumberlandgazette.co.uk%2Fnews%2Fpolitics%2Fcouncil%2Fhope-and-joyful-expectation-as-ps233m-eyemouth-primary-school-funding-agreed-9349605)[Share by Email](mailto:?subject=%E2%80%98Hope%20and%20joyful%20expectation%E2%80%99%C2%A0as%20%C2%A323.3m%20school%20funding%20is%20agreed&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.northumberlandgazette.co.uk%2Fnews%2Fpolitics%2Fcouncil%2Fhope-and-joyful-expectation-as-ps233m-eyemouth-primary-school-funding-agreed-9349605)

Published 13th Nov 2026, 12:42 GMT

## The go-ahead for funding a new £23.3million Eyemouth Primary School brings “hope and joyful expectation”, councillors have been told.

Members of [Scottish Borders Council](https://www.northumberlandgazette.co.uk/topic/scottish-borders-council) (SBC) were informed a planning application for the new school is to be submitted by March next year.

The aim is that construction would begin in October 2027, with completion one year later. Once building work is complete, the existing school and hall will be demolished.

Back in September, the wishes of the overwhelming majority of the school community won the day when SBC abandoned plans to relocate pupils into the town’s high school.

![Eyemouth Primary School.](https://www.northumberlandgazette.co.uk/webimg/b25lY21zOmViNjRlM2I2LThjOWQtNDA1NS1hZmZkLWI2MWM0OGI2ZmU3MTpmNzEyZmNkMy1iOWI0LTQ4MDAtODI1ZS1kNmQ3Y2YwZThkNWU=.jpg?crop=3:2,smart&trim=&width=640&quality=65)![placeholder image](https://www.northumberlandgazette.co.uk/img/placeholder.jpg)

Eyemouth Primary School.

Instead, it was agreed to build a new standalone primary school with early years and family centre provision on or aligned to the existing primary school site in Coldingham Road.

At full council, members were told that current capital provision available for the project is £14.3million after costs already incurred.

On the latest estimate, the additional capital requirement is therefore £8.8million.

Cllr Julie Pirone, SBC’s executive member for education, youth development and lifelong learning, said: “You will all note the costs we have to find for a new standalone school, but I want to assure parents that we will continue to push for that additional £8.8million.

“Eyemouth has been waiting a very long time for the school and I want to assure parents and the children that will be using it that they will get a school they can all be very proud of.”

East Berwickshire Conservative councillor Carol Hamilton added: “I really hope that this paper brings hope and joyful expectation to the families of Eyemouth and the surrounding communities, they have worked hard to help us with this project.

“The paper comes with a health warning, the funding is not complete and it will mean there will be some other focus for this council that may take longer down the track, but I ask my colleagues that it is time for Eyemouth, they have waited a very long time.”

The council approved a revised project budget of £23.3million excluding [VAT](https://www.northumberlandgazette.co.uk/topic/vat) which includes demolition works, risk, inflation and fees.

It also agreed to reprioritise and accelerate capital provision across the relevant financial years to meet the additional £8.8million capital requirement.

It was noted this reprioritisation will reduce the council’s capacity to commence other new capital investment.
